utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution is continuing with examination-in-chief. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday we started to -- I started to ask you questions about the exchanges, and I want to return to that topic now. In the time that you were in Batkovic, were prisoners from time to time exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And eventually did that happen to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did happen. On the 5th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken to? In other words, to what area were you released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was brought to the line between Serb Sarajevo and Sarajevo. The exact location is Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you were in Batkovic, did you see any of the accused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see on those several occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw my professor, Miro Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall on about how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where precisely did you see him on those two or three occasions? Was it inside the hangar or outside the hangar or at a location close to the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, could the witness tell us approximately what dates? Was it in 1992 that he arrived there, 1993, 1994, whatever? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard the Judge's inquiry. Can you tell the Chamber approximately when these occasions were? Think back on the period of time. If you can give us precise dates, by all means do, of course. That would be preferable. But if you can't, think back on the period of time and try and put a fix when in that period of time these two or three occasions were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the period of my imprisonment, pencils and paper were taken away from us. We only got them when we would write home through the Red Cross card. These messages were read. We were not allowed to mention important names and dates. Afterwards, these pencils were taken away from us. That is to say that I can only try to remember. Mr. Miro Tadic, my professor, came to Batkovici on several occasions until the end of 1992. I cannot recall whether it was two or three times. He brought a list of my fellow citizens from Bosanski Samac. He personally read that list, meaning who was supposed to be exchanged. Most people from the list were from the hangar; however, it would happen that some of my fellow citizens would be on the list, and these people were in their houses in Bosanski Samac. He registered this diligently, and when he returned to Bosanski Samac, as far as I know, he collected these people who were at their homes, put them on buses, and took them to lines of delineation in order to have them exchanged. As far as I can remember, this is when the religious holidays were coming up, as the end of the year would be coming up, that is to say, the 23rd, the 24th of December, 1992. I cannot recall exactly. There were faster exchanges, two or three of them, because of the religious holidays. Once I managed to get through all of this commotion through my fellow citizens. I already said that there were a lot of old people, exhausted people, young people, crippled people, and many of my fellow citizens and many citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to get to Mr. Miro Tadic. I managed somehow to pass through this throng, and I said, "Professor, I need to talk to you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you just to stop there? I'm interested in what you're about to say, but I'll get to that later. I'd just like to cast your mind back to times, okay, so that we can assist the Chamber on that inquiry about when it was that Mr. Tadic came to visit you. Now, in your last answer, you said that he came to Batkovic on several occasions until the end of 1992. You said yesterday that you were exchanged -- sorry, that you were transferred to Batkovic in late November of 1992. Is it your position that he came on these two or three occasions sometime between late November 1992 and the end of that year? Is that what your memory tells you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the period I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just permit me to just reread briefly his last answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you started to tell us about this occasion when you were able to approach Mr. Tadic, and I'd like you now to continue your narrative there. You've already described that there were a lot of people who wanted to get to him. My first question -- to get to him and speak to him. My first question is: Why did they all want to approach him and speak to him? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our understanding was that Miro Tadic could change the list, to add somebody's name to the list so that person would go and be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the two or three occasions that he came to Batkovic, did he appear to physically have a list, that is, a piece of paper with names on it? If you can tell us, please do; if you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said earlier on he had a list in his hands containing the names and surnames of my fellow citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All I want to know is if that was the case, that he had such a list on the two or three occasions that he came.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time he had a list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the occasions that he came, did you attempt to get close to him to be able to speak to him on the topic of exchanges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I got closer, I addressed him. I just said, "Professor, may I talk to you a bit?" This was already the end. The list had already been read out of the persons who were supposed to pack and go for an exchange. We went in the direction of the gate, the big iron gate. Its dimensions were about 15 by about 7 metres. The guards who were around him moved aside and the two of us walked through this iron gate into the yard. The yard had a fence all around it, a wire fence. By "wire fence," I already mentioned that. The two of us exchanged a few words and I said to him, "Professor, I am ready to give some money for helping the Serb army. Please put me on that list." He asked me, exactly, as he was looking into the ground, "Where have you got this money?" And I said to him that I haven't got any money on me, because the exchange goes through my town every time. This was the ongoing practice. When I go to town, I would borrow money from someone. He said, "All right. We'll see." And he continued walking towards the exit out of this fenced-off yard. My task was to go back to the hangar. I was awaiting the result. The last time, to the best of my knowledge, he came to the area of that camp in June 1993. I did not have an opportunity to see him. My fellow citizens say that this was the last exchange that was carried out through the Samac commission. I was disappointed, and I spent the rest of the time there. And I don't know which town it was that exchanged me and which commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This conversation that you had with Mr. Tadic, was it the only conversation that you had with him during two or three occasions that he came to Batkovic? In other words, did you not speak to him on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to get close to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact have money available to pay if things had worked out to your advantage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some money at home. It was hidden away. When leaving my town, my son, when he was leaving, he took this and everything was taken away from him, snatched away from him at the line. I have certificates to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you make this approach in this particular way, offering money? What was your reasoning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was afraid of being robbed at home. My son had stayed back, and I was already informed at the SUP, when I was detained there, by the other inmates who were brought in after me, that my wife was taken to a camp as well. So I was afraid that apartments would be searched because there was robbery and looting all over the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think perhaps you misunderstand me. My question really is directed to the issue of the money, the offer of the money. Why did you offer him money? I mean, I understand what your ultimate purpose was, but why did you choose that means to bring about your ultimate purpose of getting an exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every camp inmate, the way I saw it, could not get out. Otherwise either his family would give money or he personally would give money and then he would be put on a list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you heard from other inmates, that they would pay money to get out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard from other inmates and also from my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is what you heard from other inmates and from what you heard from your family connected with your offer of money? Is that the reason why you, you offered money to Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a lot of time to think about this, why I wasn't on the list, and as I talked about this with my other camp inmates, I came to this idea on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear from the camp inmates, the other camp inmates, as to the practice of offering money? What was your understanding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: That these people who had the misfortune of remaining at home, that they gave money in order to be put on the list and be exchanged. We who were detained could not have any money on ourselves because there were frequent searches and money was taken away from us. So if some fortunate person would have his family at home pay money for him, then he would be on the list, and that is quite well known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of such cases, such instances, in the time that you were in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you were at Batkovic, up to mid-1993 when Mr. Tadic last came, were there other men coming with lists, other men doing the same sort of job or performing the same sort of role as Mr. Tadic or was he the only one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other accused who are here, I never saw them there, and I didn't hear of them coming there. However, other teams did come. They read lists, and they took detained people from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time that you were in Batkovic, did you get any news of your wife's whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was registered the first time, after the 11th of August, as being a camp inmate, on the 13th of December the following thing happened: It was the first time I got a little piece of paper and a pencil giving me the right to write to my family. To the best of my knowledge, my family was no longer in Samac. I could not remember any other addresses. So I wondered who I should write to. I talked about this to the gentlemen from the Red Cross, and they said to me that I should write the name and surname of my daughter, [redacted] [redacted], and that they would try to find her. That is what I did. That was my first contact with the world, through a piece of paper and a pencil, on the 13th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So, Witness, at the end of the day, did you pay any money to Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not, because I got out in 1994, and to the best of my knowledge, he was not coming after the month of June 1993. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time you came to be exchanged in October 1994, were there many Bosanski Samac people left in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was taken to the line of delineation, as far as I can remember, there were about 20 of us camp inmates. About 40 stayed behind after me, who were still detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got any idea as to why it was that you were chosen to go on that particular date? In other words, was there any rhyme or reason as to October 1994 as opposed to June 1994 or some other day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that only God brought this joy to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after you were exchanged? Did you stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I got out into the besieged Sarajevo, a transporter took me. I think the transporter belonged to the UN. This lasted quite awhile. However, the drive was only 500 metres. When I got out to some kind of freedom, I thought that this was unreal. So for a long time, I walked around a table where I was supposed to give my name and surname, my year of birth and to say where I was from. I was brought to another town which was unknown to me then because that town had changed completely. When I came to a bit, I registered there, and I asked these gentlemen who were working there on exchanges, or to be more precise, Amor Masovic was there then. "Sir, I came to Sarajevo several times. Tell me where is the centre? In which direction is the Cengic Vila?" Because from earlier on, I had my brother there, Cengic Vila, and I had intended to go to his place. Everything seemed foreign to me. There weren't any trees around me. Houses had been destroyed. There was nothing lively about the place. Sarajevo was an empty town. Later on, I found out that these people who were in Sarajevo were praying to God to get out of town. To the best of my knowledge, Sarajevo was besieged, and there were three encirclements around it: sniper shooters, tanks, mortars. Every day, including that day, as far as I can remember, we were shelled in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio. I was about to ask where we were going. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, I just want to know: Were you eventually reunited with your family? I just want to know when, if and when that occurred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken, and I will find this out later, to the command of the 1st Corps, where I gave them my information: who I am, where I'm from, my date of birth. And I told him, "I have a brother," and they called him immediately on the telephone. And at the first moment, we couldn't even recognise one another. He had lost a lot of weight. He was deformed, and most probably this is how I looked to him as well. We exchanged a few words. We were not able to stand. We went towards his house under a rain of bullets, a shower of bullets. When I got to the house, I had difficulty recognising everything. His two daughters were with him. We didn't have anything to eat that day. However, we were happy because we were beginning to come together again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you reunited with your wife eventually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't possible to call. There was no possibility. However, some phone numbers -- or some telephones, which I didn't know before, were at the Presidency, so my brother took me there and we told them about my case, and they made it possible to get in touch with my wife from the Presidency building, with my wife who was with my daughter in Austria. I told her that I was released, and she asked, "What have you decided?" And I said, knowing the situation in Sarajevo, the hunger, the exhaustion, the siege, it was not possible to leave Sarajevo, but I was offered by the UNPROFOR, the Red Cross, and the government to take me out. Sarajevo looked big to me. Most probably, after that hangar and that cell where I spent 27 and a half months, I didn't want to leave Sarajevo. My wife took her bags and she came to Sarajevo. She entered beneath the ground, through some tunnel, which I will later use on many occasions. We remained there the whole time, until the news in the year 2000, in the month of October, when the Serbian government decided to return my property to me, which was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: And within 20 days, I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I cut you off. Within 20 days you did what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I packed, and on my own expense, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]. That's how I estimate the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give us a brief description, please, of the state of [redacted] when you returned. What sort of condition was it in, was it being used, that sort of thing. And just make it brief, okay? We just need a brief summary of what's happened in respect of your property, and we'll start with [redacted], okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at Bosanski Samac, [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the name of this lady?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much rent did she pay to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received a single dinar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I'm advised because of the difficulties of spotting identifying matters of the witness, maybe we move into private session now that we appear to be closing in on his family. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm grateful for that. I'm sorry. Once again, it escaped my mind, and I'm grateful to the Chamber for reminding me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Zecevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I'm attorney Slobodan Zecevic. I will ask you some questions. And I kindly ask you, and I will also try to formulate my questions in such a way, that you respond with "yes," "no," or, "I don't know," to my questions if you don't know. Sir, let's go back a little bit in relation to the questions that were asked you by the Prosecutor. I would like to take you back to the fire at [redacted]. If you remember, on page 6, line 16 of the unofficial transcript, you explained that an article appeared in the [redacted] magazine, if I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it wasn't some article. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So yes, there was an article in the [redacted] magazine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was an article in the [redacted] magazine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can I remind the witness, please, since you're speaking the same language with counsel, do remember to pause before you answer counsel's questions, because the interpreters have to complete interpreting the question by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript, when you paraphrase the contents of that article from the [redacted] magazine, you said that it was something in -- along the general lines of there was another burning in Bosanski Samac and another explosion on such-and-such a day. Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another burning, [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me to read it back to you. I will read it in English because the transcript is in English. [In English] "Yes. Time at the beginning of 1992, an article appeared in a weekly paper [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]. And there was a photograph and also an article on one page with a general -- I cannot tell -- I cannot tell you the general sense of the whole article word by word, but it went something like this: `In Bosanski Samac, there's been another burning and another explosion on such-and-such date. A weekend house and a farm burned down owned by -- it burned down. It is assumed that there were weapons there, that the owner held SDA weapons at that location.'" [Interpretation] Did you state this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. It was assumed that there were arms there. This is what I stated, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me -- you also mention an explosion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mention an explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an explosion or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I wasn't there. The firefighters and the MUP were there, and they have an official report. [redacted] [redacted] the firefighters were concerned that this would blow up and hurt other people, and this is stated in the official report on this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to read another portion from your testimony of yesterday. This is a section of the unofficial transcript, page 32, line 7 onwards: [In English] "Now that I remember, and when I analyse, my town seemed more like a barracks to me, a barracks that was within firing range, and also the target of other weapons, so that the separation line, the line of separation, was in direction of [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted], so that we lived inside as if we were exposed to constant shelling." [Interpretation] Is it true? Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, sir: What you stated was something that referred to the entire town of Bosanski Samac or it only referred to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the entire town of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This means so that the town was practically encircled and was targeted the entire time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was encircled. It was encircled, and we were a target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was constantly shelled; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that this referred to the whole town, I assume you mean that it included all of the citizens of that town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did include all of the citizens of that town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This shelling and this feeling that you had, is that what you meant when at one point, on page 37, line 10, you said: [In English] "At every moment, from the 17th of April until I was released, until I was sort of set free, I was exposed to danger"? [Interpretation] Did you mean this also? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that too. That was also one of the reasons. Because it would happen that my citizens, my fellow citizens in the town of Samac, would be killed in the yards of their homes or in the rooms where we were held, where we were detained in the SUP and TO buildings. Many of them were killed in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From shells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: From shells. According to my information, a number of children and women were also victims of the shells, women who were not active, and also a large number of civilians. Some of those civilians were also being held at the TO and the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding your work in April of 1992 and onwards, you stated, on page 31, line 25 of the unofficial transcript from yesterday, you stated the following: [In English] "We would load those sandbags into a truck and then used them to protect certain buildings in Samac, like the municipal building. We would also place these sandbags in front or behind windows, as a parapet." [Interpretation] Is this what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: The building of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac, it's in the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right by the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other side of the river is Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is one of the places from which Bosanski Samac was shelled; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, if you can remember: How high up did you put these sandbags on the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three rows from the window sill, so there could be a bit of light inside the building as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May the usher please show the photograph -- I believe it's P14, and the photograph is number F46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: P14A, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: P14A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zecevic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've been clicking it off and on. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a bit of a task. We have to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please tell me: Is this the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the municipality building in my town of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to use the pointer and show us how high up these sandbags went on the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to avail myself of this opportunity, now that I've been given the floor. This is the building, and 300 metres away from it, over here, is this Spomen Dom. That was surrounded by sand. We loaded sand into bags and we put it in, and then we loaded the sandbags into the little truck owned by Hurtic. The little truck transported sand up to the municipality building. Then we took these sandbags and then we went through the hall and then we went to the fourth or fifth door there. I know the municipality as well as I know my own pocket. This window here and this window there were for the president of the municipality at that time. That's what people talked amongst us. And this was for Milan Simic. That's what people were saying. And it was nicely decorated inside. There was also a TV set, tables, things like that. Three or four rows we placed there, to the best of my knowledge, because the sandbags were longer than the window sill, so they were a bit folded. So then we put three or four sandbags up to the half of the window, and then there would be some room left towards the top of the window so that light could get in. If necessary, I can clarify this more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did you put the sandbags inside as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went in through the building and then we put the sandbags there. Some people helped from the outside so that they would not fall off; and those who had the task of working inside, there was an open window, and then we placed these sandbags on the window sill on the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I manage to understand what you've been saying, it is only the upper part of the window that was used for bringing sunlight in; all the rest was covered by sandbags.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my estimate is that the sandbags took up about half of the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These sandbags prevented light from coming in and sound; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. These sandbags were there for saving people, because the shells would fall there from the line of separation. So it was because of shrapnel, so that shrapnel could not fall directly into the building. That is why these sandbags were put there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have understood that, but I'm asking you, to the best of your knowledge: These sandbags that were used as protection from shrapnel also prevented light and sound from getting into the buildings; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these sandbags probably did that. There was less light in these facilities, and also there was less noise, if they managed to give that kind of protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the usher please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zecevic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you please show the witness the photograph number F56.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is the SUP yard, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Slobodan, this is the yard of the SUP building where I was locked up for three and a half months, underneath from where this picture is, or, rather, three metres down are the windows where I was detained for three months. I kept looking through this window all the time. Oh, yes. This is the location of the SUP yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wished to know only. Tell me, towards the top you can see some willows and the river. Is that the Sava?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Slobodan Zecevic, these willows were full of communication trenches where Serb soldiers were. And since I had the opportunity of digging these trenches and cleaning them, these other willows towards the top, they have other parapets and other trenches. Who was digging for them and who was there at that time, I didn't know at the time. That is territory of the previous Croatia and nowadays of the State of Croatia. Between these two rows of poplars is my Sava River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please use the pointer and point out the Sava River and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sava is here. Croatia is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in the left-hand corner of this photograph, we can also see a prefabricated building. This prefabricated building, is it in fact in the yard of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before, these were garages that were intended for parking vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please point all of this out on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of these garages were made previously, before the 17th of April, and they were used to park vehicles. And when the 17th of April happened, many were used for detaining my fellow citizens. So in garage number 4, there were two of my fellow citizens detained in there, and they spent all of their time there while I was at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I really do not wish to interrupt you. I beg your pardon. But I just asked you about the prefabricated building in the left-hand corner of the picture. That is in the yard of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying building number 1?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. See in the left-hand corner, you can see a roof and some windows? Yes, that's it. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is part of the municipality building, of the municipal assembly building. That is where the land surveyors were, those who measured our ploughing fields and our houses and all the property we had before 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that this is where the land surveyors were before the 17th of April, 1992? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this building was used at all after the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many buildings like the municipal assembly that we saw awhile ago were moved to safer locations. I personally, sometime in the month of June 1992 while I was still apparently free, from the attic of the municipal assembly building, I collected documents and carried them to the premises downstairs, the second room on the left-hand side. When you enter through the entrance door of my municipal assembly, that's where it is. We talked about this, but it seemed that it was to prevent these documents from having a shell fall on top of that building and then burning all of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I could ask the witness -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: -- a question. Witness, could you tell the Chamber whether the prefabricated building on the left of the picture also had sandbags halfway up the windows there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to this building here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not enter that building during the course of the war. I don't know whether there were sandbags there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Just one question following from that. Looking at that picture, you pointed out the Sava River, the trenches on this side of the Sava River, your side, and then the barricades on the other side of the Sava River, the barricades of the Croats. Now, when you refer to the sandbags being placed there for protective measure, was it from the shells coming from the Croat side across the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shells were coming from all sides, shells unknown to me. I said before where the separation line was in my town. It was driven through, so to speak. So I'm going to repeat this. On the left-hand side, in my estimate, about 500 metres away from my house which is in the centre of town; or from this location, 700 metres as the crow flies, from the western side; on the northern side, 150 metres. From the eastern side, 2 to 3 kilometres. I don't know exactly where they were coming from, but they were coming every day from all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: My specific question was: Did shells also come from the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a civilian at that time, I had concluded that they were coming from that side, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed? Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, tell me, do you remember -- since we're on the subject of shelling, do you remember that the Croatian air force attacked Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, sir, I had already been detained, but I heard, because news spread quickly amongst us, that some aircraft had come either in October or November, to the best of my knowledge. And we laughed a bit. That's what they told us, that that side did not have any weapons. It was an agriculture aircraft that had come and that had thrown gas canisters that were full of dynamite and pieces of iron, and they exploded in my town, the location of the street that was formerly called Ivo Lola Ribar. [redacted]. [redacted]. And this location is near the waterworks, the waterworks that supplied our town with water, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm going to read another portion of your statement from yesterday to you. Just bear with me for a second, please. [In English] "As we were passing by, if we were going on foot, it was very, very difficult to move because there were frequent checks in the town." [Interpretation] Can you hear me, sir? [In English] "And they were practically capturing Muslims and Croats only because their name wasn't right. And they would take them to the municipal building. And all of us citizens knew that, so that even when we were going home on our way back from work, then we will hide." [Interpretation] Is this what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, something to that effect, like what it was -- like what was interpreted to me right now. I don't know whether that is what was written down as well, but if necessary, I can repeat all of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just interested in this, what you said, the municipal assembly. Have you referred to the municipal assembly building or some other building? Could you please tell me what you meant if you meant another building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, sir, we are going to show you a document now that was shown to you yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Show the Witness P35, please. I believe that's the order which the Prosecutor produced yesterday. It's P35, according to my knowledge. Maybe it's a different number. I have it over here. Mr. Usher, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Usually when we have already got the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I wrote "P35," but I believe with --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thirty-six.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-six. Yes. That's why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So the correct number is P36.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, please take a look at this document that is in front of you in the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this order pertained to all persons, all citizens of Bosanski Samac; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order I never had in my hands, but often I heard through the mass media in Bosanski Samac. I don't know what this referred to or who this referred to, but most probably everybody had to observe this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to look at it, look at this order? Please read the text. I mean, you don't have to read it out loud. Read it to yourself. We have an English version here. Just tell me whether there is anything that states ethnic background or something like that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I did not come here to prove anything. I came here to say this. Namely, what I heard and saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Witness, you answer the questions put to you by counsel. If you don't know, you say so. If you can't tell by looking at this document and answer the question put to you by counsel, you say so. I do agree with you that you may not be able to interpret documents. So you simply say you don't know or you can't tell. Don't be rude to counsel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise if that is how I have been understood. However, behind your back is a large number of my fellow citizens. I believe that they all knew that. Those previous prohibitions as far as ethnic background is concerned, on the 17th of April, this remains imprinted in my memory. Also this order that I see here in front of me, I think that it related only to Bosniaks and Croats, because during the curfew hours, the citizens of Serb ethnicity had to hold the lines and move about town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I just asked you to tell me whether in this document there is anything stating that this refers to citizens of Croat and Muslim ethnicity or not, or whether it pertains to all citizens; just that, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document pertains to all citizens of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when you talked about that certificate that you got three or four days later, after the 17th of April, actually, in 1992, you said that you came to the Uniglas building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over there, there were some other people who were waiting. You said that they were all of Serb ethnicity; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked to them. Were they also seeking such certificates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity of talking to them for about four or five minutes, and they were seeking these certificates too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Like you, these were people who had some business there, and that's what they needed these certificates for; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were citizens of Serb ethnicity. They wore camouflage uniforms. They did not have any weapons. I don't know what their business was. Like my fellow citizen Laza Devetka, who needed a certificate to get some business done in Serbia. I don't know what his business was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me: When you entered this room where you saw Milan Simic, you said in the transcript that with him, Mr. Jovanovic -- there was Mr. Jovanovic with him too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Mirko Jovanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Oh, I'm sorry. I don't know his name, but I shall describe him, so if necessary, my fellow citizens will know who he is. Before the 17th of April, he was head of the economic department in the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac. He wore a beard. I don't know where he was from. I think he was from the territory of Orasje. However, he had got a job in Bosanski Samac perhaps a year or a year and a half before the war operations started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was head of the economic department in Bosanski Samac before the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I introduced him properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just clarify one thing, please: This person whom you saw in that room, with the last name of Jovanovic, was head of the economic department in Bosanski Samac in the municipality of Bosanski Samac before the 17th of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is to say that he worked in the Municipal Assembly. He was the second person there in terms of importance, in terms of the categories involved. It was the president of the municipality and then him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me: You know Milan Simic and his family well; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Milan work as a clerk for this Mr. Jovanovic at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, let me ask you something else now. You discussed that yesterday with the Prosecutor during your examination. As far as I can remember, you did your military service, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did my military service in 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, you were a reserve military conscript, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my war assignment, wartime assignment, that if war were to break out, I was supposed to report [redacted]. I was not a member of the TO until the 16th of April, 1992. I had a wartime assignment. That's the way things were in our country. Everybody knew where they were supposed to report. I was supposed to report at [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was the place -- that was the wartime assignment that you had before 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this company, at [redacted], that's where you worked; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have worked there for a long number of years; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of December, 1969.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You started working then and you've been working there from then onwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, since you worked in this state-owned enterprise and you had your wartime assignment there, et cetera, do you know that work obligation in case of an immediate threat of war or threat of war was the obligation of each and every citizen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. It was the obligation of each and every citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This obligation was general, wasn't it, except for those who were military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question, but I agree with you that that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I put this question to you, I was referring to the following. Let me just explain this to you in order to prevent any misunderstandings. Work obligation was general, whereas military obligation pertained to those who had wartime assignments, that is to say, military-aged men between the ages of 18 and 60; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you were involved in the military obligation, if you had a wartime assignment, then you did not have a work obligation; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My wartime assignment was to report at the gasoline station, because this was of military significance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, if you remember: In 1992, did you want to join the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had already been there. I considered myself to belong to the JNA units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain how you considered this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in some JNA unit in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see it's 11.00. Maybe it's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break and resume at 1130 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will continue later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome, Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The cross-examination is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just one request. I've been warned by the interpreters, so please wait until my question is completely interpreted and then begin with your answer. I will try to be as slow as possible, and I would ask you also to do the same. The interpreters work very hard, and we need to give them time to translate everything that's being said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understood. I will try to fit in. It's not -- I'm not used to sitting here and answering questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, please tell me: On the 16th of April, you joined the TO of the BH; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th of April, 1992. I joined as soon as I received a weapon. I joined the TO of the BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go back to some documents that the Prosecutor showed you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would the usher please show the Witness P39 ter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You remember the document from yesterday, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a list of names from 1 to 9, the names of my fellow citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: In column number 3, under the column -- under the title "Work post," their duties, their work is stated, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you know the gentleman under number 2. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my fellow citizen Dzevad Celic, and [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the gentleman under number 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my fellow citizen Sejfudin Sejdinovic. [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do know him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me if you know whether this group of nine people made up the list of people for work obligation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they did or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the title, it says: "The clerks and others, DR, for the brigades." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me what is the usual job, the usual work of the clerks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: The clerks, as far as I know, work with pens and paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, could you please tell me the following: In your previous statement, you said that as far as you know, the gentleman under number 2, your family friend, did not work as a clerk up until the 11th of August, i.e. up until the date that you were detained.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dzevad Celic went with me to the work assignments several times. He wasn't working as a clerk until the 11th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I have the document number 1, which I -- Your Honours, I would like to introduce a document and be marked for identification. Actually, this is -- this is the payment list of the reference typists, the couriers, and the other couriers who are working on the organisation of work in the working brigade. That's the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: During the period --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During the period from April until August. Actually, if I may just assist the Court. When I disclosed the document P39 ter to the Prosecutor, this document was actually the second page of that document when I disclosed it to the -- yesterday the Prosecutor used this page only, and this second page is basically referring to the first page. But in any case, I would like to introduce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we haven't had that page which you call the second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We haven't received that page which you call the second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You haven't seen it. I'm just now introducing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So we can have it marked for identification only. It hasn't got the official English translation, not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I'm afraid not, not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For identification purposes only.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The identification number will be D23/2 ter. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, might I just cross the courtroom and confer with my colleague? I'd like to make sure that I've got the same document in my hand that he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Because I can't tell. I suspect I've got the right one, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. We sorted that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you kindly read the title of the document, on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Payment list of the clerk, typist, courier, summons courier, and those working to organise the work in the work brigade."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please read the clerk, item number 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here the name Dzevad Celic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you once again to pause between my question and before you begin your answer. After the name and the surname under number 2, in continuation, there are some numbers which pertain to certain months.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They pertain to April, May, June, July, and August. Total time, total amount, and also remarks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: These numbers under item 2 - 4, 26, 31?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Total number of days, 61.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand this to mean that these are the days that the gentleman under item 2 spent on work duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that as meaning that Dzevad Celic spent 61 days over the past five months as a clerk, working as a clerk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you claim that this is not true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Celic Dzevad did not work as a clerk until the 11th of April. When I was taken into the SUP building, I heard from my fellow citizens who were brought in after me that Mr. Dzevad Celic was working on those duties which are more or less described in the heading of the document. I firmly claim that Dzevad Celic was not a clerk. I have proof of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, can you just wait? The witness mentioned the 11th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That was what I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Could you clarify that with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said the 11th of April. Did you mean the 11th of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I meant the 11th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please also read to me, if you see it on this copy, what it says at the bottom of the page, where the signature is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]. That is the name of my fellow citizen and also my school friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the gentleman who is on this list under item number 1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Above his signature, it states "certified by."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that, according to you, do you understand this to mean that the information that is in this document was verified [redacted] [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather say that he falsified this information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you properly, you allow for the possibility that some of these documents are incomplete because they pertained to the months of April to August, but they were compiled in November. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not what I meant. I meant that specifically Dzevad Celic was not a clerk, and I have proof for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that the same mistake could have appeared in some other documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's possible for mistakes to creep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind to show the witness two documents simultaneously: D22E/2 ter and P37 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: D22E/2 ter and P37 ter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you were shown yesterday or the day before both of these documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that these documents were shown to me. I can see the names and the surnames of my fellow citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm only interested in the following: Could you kindly read the heading of the document that you are holding in your hand, and that is D22E/2 ter. Could you just please read the heading.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: "List of workers engaged in the work brigade for the months of April, May, June, July, and August 1992."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you kindly read the heading of the second document, and that is the document P37 ter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: "List of the workers engaged in the work brigade for the months of April, May, June, July, and August 1992."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: "Payroll list of the workers engaged," and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if there is anything above what you have just read to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Supplemental." "Supplemental payroll list."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you take this as a document which can be attached to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot claim something like that. I don't have any reason to claim that, because the previous document has been certified on the last page. The earlier, previous pages are not certified anywhere, and this document here is certified. And I would say that it belonged to some other document which is not certified at the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it says "Supplemental payroll list," does that usually indicate that information has been added which was not included in a previous document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it means to me as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Usher, you can take the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, yesterday during the examination-in-chief, you said the following, and I will read it back to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I'm so sorry to intervene at this stage. You asked him a question that P37 was supplemental to D22E.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I assume you have checked both lists and all the 11 names are indeed D22E.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Are all the 11 names in D22E?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: You see, you've got 11 names in P37, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: And this is supplemental you put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And they're already included in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Yes. Are they all in D22E?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know, Your Honour. Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I'm asking you to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. I'm sorry. I didn't understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: No, no. I'm asking you to confirm if all these names are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to check it out, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Then you must check this out before you even ask him the question, because if it's not, then it cannot be supplemental.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So can you check it out now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Please bear with me. Your Honours, what I was referring is that this document, by its title, says "Additional list." That was the only purpose of my questions, that this is additional list. What I'm trying to explain to this Honourable Trial Chamber is that the lists are not complete. So there are some additional lists, because people who are working on that probably missed some of the people who were -- who are not on the original list. That was the only purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So the words "Additional payment" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So the words "Additional payment" on the top does not mean additional payment to those persons to whom payment is set out in D22E.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. It means additional people which have not been included in this list, the previous -- D22E/2 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Additional names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Additional names. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me read to you what you stated earlier. This is unofficial transcript page 42, line 10 onwards:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doing the best you can -- [In English] This is the question posed to you from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And please read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doing the best you can, about how many people did you hear of being killed in the way that you've described between April and August when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said two or three men. Several persons were wounded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Slobodan Zecevic, which people did you mean, those who were detained at the SUP or those who were working in the communication trenches or those who were in the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the witness is right to ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but I haven't posed the question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness was answering to me before I posed the question to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. You hadn't completed. Because it's fair to tell him about which aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. It was my intention, but I didn't finish the question and I didn't want to cut short the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. I think maybe you can go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. We probably misunderstood one another. I meant the following: You responded to this question when you were talking about the people who were killed -- while -- killed or wounded while carrying out their work obligation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understood the question. According to my estimate, two to three men were killed while performing the jobs of digging the communication trenches or cutting the grass in front of the communication trenches. So two or three of my fellow citizens were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would the usher please show the witness P38 ter document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You looked at this document yesterday, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document was before me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, under the heading "Killed," how many numbers are there and how many names of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, three people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is in accordance with what you told us a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the heading "Wounded," how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under that column, "Wounded," four of the citizens from my town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your information, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many that were wounded. There were many more wounded and there were many more killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm only thinking -- I'm only limiting myself to those persons who were in the work brigades.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are thinking of the work brigades, when we were taken out from the camps, then I would add, sir, Slobodan Zecevic, that many more of my fellow citizens were killed while digging trenches and carrying out forced labour jobs than there are on this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see that we will have to clarify this. The document that is in front of you pertains to the months of April through August 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says "workers in the work brigade" in the heading, and then it says, in brackets, "killed or wounded"; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few minutes ago you confirmed that the number of killed persons corresponds to what you remember and what you know; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you about the number of wounded persons. Does that match what you know? If you don't know, just say "I don't know," and if you do know, say either "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that it corresponds to your own knowledge; this which is written in this document corresponds to what you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very importantly, you did not ask me whether it pertains to these four or five months. You asked me, to the best of my knowledge, whether I agree with the number of persons wounded who were in the work brigades. I said that I did not agree. However, when I see this document, for all these months, to the best of my knowledge, yes, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. My mistake. I shall try to be clearer in the future. I do apologise. Let us just finish with this document. So in your opinion, the facts mentioned in this document are true, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I could be informed of such matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir: Yesterday when you were answering the Prosecutor's questions in relation to work obligation, a few times you said that you did not know about some persons whose names were read out here, whether they were involved in work obligation or not; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that work obligation, as I said, was of a general nature and that it existed in all companies in Bosanski Samac that were operating at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I not been aware of that, that everybody had work obligation, I would not have responded to each and every call-up when we were supposed to go into action [as interpreted]. I would have stayed sitting at home, thinking that it was not my obligation to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The witness has said -- it's 48, 4. He said "to go into working action" and not "the action."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, so you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask the witness again to clarify that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To clarify, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that there is a mistake in the transcript, a small one. You said that, "Had I not been aware of that, that everybody had work obligation, I would not have responded to each and every call-up when we were supposed to go into working action." Is that what you said, "work action"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the way I put it. God gave it to all of us. God gave us all eyes, ears, and the power of speech. We are all not the same as far as play with words is concerned. I was referring to forced labour that we went to do every day. There is a possibility that I make a mistake in the future as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in companies like the Samac textile industry, there were people who were working in terms of work obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that firm, and I always tried to sidestep it, because this is where Serb soldiers were staying, those who wore uniforms, and whoever went there would return with bruises. When Serb soldiers would find out that this person was of Muslim ethnicity, then my fellow citizens would sometimes be beaten up at that facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know then, for example, in the company of Master, did you know that there was work obligation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS L [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. A fellow citizen of mine was working there, and he tried, day after day, as he was going to work obligation at Master, to give us some food while we were detained at the SUP. We were fortunate because his brother was among us. During the first 15 days or so, I was in front -- I was in the front part of the SUP building in Bosanski Samac.
